articles.title: NTA Floats Rs 7.5 Crore Tender for Round-the-Clock Security at Delhi HQ and Regional Offices
articles.description: Following the NEET-UG 2026 controversy, the National Testing Agency has floated a Rs 7.5 crore tender for 24/7 security at its Delhi headquarters and regional offices.

articles.title: Union Cabinet approves Sudhmahadev-Dranga, Singhpora-Vailoo tunnel projects: DrJitendra
articles.description: Jammu, Aug 1: Union Cabinet has approved the strategically crucial uni-directional twin tube Sudhmahadev–Dranga and the twin tube Singhpora–Vailoo tunnel projects with approach roads on NH-244 in Jammu and Kashmir, at a total cost of Rs 9779.42 Cr. Approval was granted to these projects in the union cabinet meeting, chaired by the Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Friday, July 31, 2026. Union Minister of State in PMO DrJitendra Singh, while announcing it on his social media handle on Saturday, expressed his gratitude to the Prime Minister for the cabinet approval to these ambitious tunnel projects in his Lok Sabha constituency. He also thanked the Union Minister of Road Transport and Highways (MoRTH) Nitin Gadkari for facilitating it. DrJitendra represents the Doda-Kathua-Udhampur parliamentary constituency in Lok Sabha. Fully Centre-funded Sudhmahadev–Dranga and Singhpora–Vailoo tunnel projects with their approach roads on Anantnag-Chenani corridor will bolster road connectivity in Udhampur and Chenab valley districts. In mid-April this year, uni-directional twin tube Sudhmahadev–Dranga tunnel (length 12.85 km, including 2 L (lane) plus Paved Shoulder (PS) approaches) and the twin tube Singhpora–Vailoo tunnel (length 38.61 km, including 2L plus PS approaches) on NH-244 received an official approval through an Office Memorandum issued by the (Union) Ministry of Finance, Department of Expenditure, confirming the minutes of the Public Investment Board (PIB) meeting held on April 7, 2026, thereby formalising the transformative project. “My heartfelt gratitude to PM Sh @narendramodi Ji for the cabinet approval of the landmark 9800 Cr Sudhmahadev–Dranga and Singhpora–Vailoo tunnel projects on NH-244 in my Lok Sabha constituency. This visionary decision is a defining milestone in the transformation of Jammu and Kashmir’s transport infrastructure and a testament to the government’s unwavering commitment to balanced regional development,” DrJitendra posted, with a screenshot of a national daily report about the cabinet’s approval to the projects. Union Minister of State in PMO asserted that the strategically significant projects would “provide seamless all-weather connectivity between Jammu and the Kashmir valley while substantially improving access to the Chenab region.” “By bypassing road stretches vulnerable to landslides, snowfall and adverse weather, the tunnels will enhance road safety, reduce travel time, improve disaster resilience, strengthen strategic and defence mobility and ensure uninterrupted movement of people, goods and essential services throughout the year,” he stated. Beyond infrastructure, DrJitendra said, “This initiative will unlock unprecedented opportunities for economic growth, tourism, trade, employment and social development, bringing lasting benefits to the people of Doda, Kishtwar, Ramban, Udhampur and the entire Union Territory.” While thanking Union Minister MoRTH, he described the initiative as a “visionary investment in the future of J&K and a significant stride towards a stronger, safer and more connected India.” Later, DrJitendra, while speaking to media persons on the sidelines of an official function in Kathua on Saturday, August 1, 2026, stated during last one year, misleading reports were carried about the Sudhmahadev tunnel that the project was cancelled. He clarified that reports about stoppage of work were incorrect. The Union Minister said the earlier tender was cancelled because of the security issue related to the allottee. He said that later a new tender was floated and on July 31, 2026, the Union Cabinet approved the tunnel projects. With regard to the Chhatergala tunnel project, DrJitendra informed that it was taken up in the plan – Vision 2047 document. “We are trying to include it in our next five-year plan as it would take longer to complete it. But once completed, it would provide round the year connectivity and would thus prove to be a game changer for the region. Because presently it becomes a hideout for terrorists during extreme weather conditions when the road gets closed,” the Union Minister of State in PMO said. Notably, the Chief Minister Omar Abdullah too had recently written to the Prime Minister Narendra Modi and the Union Minister for Road Transport and Highways Nitin Gadkari seeking early completion of both the projects. Prior to it, on March 25, 2026, the Union Minister of Road Transport and Highways Nitin Gadkari, while replying to National Conference MP Sajjad Ahmad Kichloo’s question in Rajya Sabha about the present status, DPR, tendering, land acquisition, environment and security clearances, funds sanctioned and released, work awarded and timeline fixed for the projects related to the Sudhmahadev-Chenani tunnel, Singhpora-Vailoo tunnel besides other tunnels and road projects had informed that DPRs were completed for both the projects. “Sudhmahadev-Dranga and Singhpora-Vailoo tunnels fall under National Highway (NH) 244. The Detailed Project Reports (DPRs) for these tunnels have been completed by National Highways Infrastructure Development Company Limited (NHIDCL),” Gadkari had stated. “The Sudhmahadev-Daranga tunnel including approaches is having a length of 12.85 km and Singhpora-Vailoo tunnel including approaches is having a length of 38.61 km. The projects for construction of these tunnels are at appraisal stage,” the Union Minister of Road Transport and Highways had informed. Regarding road projects, Gadkari had informed that the road stretch of Batote-Doda-Kishtwar is divided into two stretches. “The Batote-Khellani section of NH-244 is of 2-lane standards. However, due to deficient alignment having steep curves, this stretch is to be bypassed through development of Chenani-Sudhmahadev-Goha-Khellanigreenfield alignment. Out of total length of 38 km from Chenani to Khellani (excluding Sudhmadev-Dranga tunnel portion) the 2-lane has been completed in 34 km and 2-laning is in progress in the remaining 4 km, which is scheduled to be completed by October, 2026,” he said. “The Khellani-Doda-Kishtwar section of NH-244 (112.66 km) is being developed to 2-lane with paved shoulders configuration in 9 civil work contract packages, of which, 47.38 km length has been completed and remaining length is in progress,” Gadkari had shared.

articles.title: SIDBI and India’s MSME Development: The Case for a Larger Last-Mile Role
articles.description: India’s apex MSME financial institution has built a formidable lending and development ecosystem. The next opportunity is to use these strengths more visibly and extensively at the level of individual micro and small enterprises. India’s Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises occupy a central position in the country’s economic development. According to the Ministry of MSME’s Annual Report 2025-26, the sector contributes approximately 31.1 per cent of India’s GDP and more than 48.5 per cent of the country’s exports. It also supports entrepreneurship, employment generation and industrial activity across urban, semi-urban and rural India. Within this ecosystem, the Small Industries Development Bank of India has a distinctive and important responsibility. SIDBI was established under an Act of Parliament in 1990 and is mandated to function as the principal financial institution for the promotion, financing and development of the MSME sector . Its mandate also includes coordinating with institutions engaged in similar activities. Over the years, SIDBI has developed a significant institutional presence in MSME finance, credit guarantees, venture funding, digital lending, cluster development, refinancing and entrepreneurship promotion. This editorial does not question SIDBI’s intent, integrity or contribution. Nor does it suggest that the challenges faced by MSMEs can be attributed to one institution. The argument is narrower and constructive: given SIDBI’s mandate, financial strength, institutional knowledge and position within the MSME ecosystem, there is considerable scope for it to play an even larger and more visible last-mile role. SIDBI Has Built a Strong Foundation A balanced assessment must recognise the scale of SIDBI’s contribution. SIDBI reported loans and advances of approximately ₹4.96 lakh crore at the end of FY2024-25. Its direct-lending portfolio increased by 41 per cent during the year, rising from ₹26,826 crore to ₹37,781 crore. Its branch network stood at 127 offices. The institution has also helped develop or support several important components of India’s MSME financial architecture. Its work covers indirect lending through banks, small finance banks, NBFCs, microfinance institutions and financial-technology companies; direct lending through demonstrative and innovative products; Fund of Funds initiatives; credit-plus development programmes; and implementation support for government schemes. SIDBI’s contribution must therefore be assessed as more than the value of loans sanctioned directly by its branches. Its interventions influence a broader network of lenders, platforms, funds and development institutions. That multiplier role remains valuable and should continue. The policy question, however, is whether the balance between wholesale financial support and direct developmental engagement should evolve further as the requirements of Indian MSMEs become more complex. Understanding the Institutional-Finance Model According to SIDBI’s FY2024-25 Annual Report, institutional finance represented approximately 92 per cent of the bank’s loans and advances, with outstanding institutional finance of ₹4.55 lakh crore. Direct lending stood at ₹37,781 crore. This composition should not automatically be interpreted as a weakness. Indirect lending allows SIDBI to use the existing networks of banks, NBFCs, small finance banks, microfinance institutions and fintech companies. It can generate a multiplier effect and potentially reach many more enterprises than SIDBI could serve independently. At the same time, the predominance of institutional finance raises legitimate policy questions that deserve discussion. For example: How much of the benefit arising from SIDBI’s lower-cost or development-oriented funding is ultimately passed on to the MSME borrower? Are first-time borrowers and very small enterprises receiving an adequate share of the credit supported by SIDBI? Are MSMEs located outside major commercial centres benefiting proportionately? Are partner institutions financing enterprises that would otherwise have struggled to obtain formal credit? These questions do not imply that SIDBI or its partner institutions are failing. They are questions about measuring developmental additionality alongside conventional financial performance. The purpose of such an assessment should be to strengthen the existing model rather than replace it. The MSME Credit Gap Remains a Systemic Challenge India’s MSME credit environment has improved substantially, particularly through formalisation, digital lending, credit guarantees and greater availability of commercial data. Nevertheless, a SIDBI study based on interactions with more than 2,000 MSMEs across 19 sectors estimated the MSME credit gap at approximately ₹30 lakh crore. The report also identified challenges involving formal credit, technology adoption, infrastructure, market access, compliance and skilled labour. This estimate reflects a system-wide challenge. Responsibility for closing the gap is shared among central and state governments, commercial banks, NBFCs, fintech companies, credit-guarantee institutions, large corporate buyers and the MSMEs themselves. It would therefore be incorrect to present the credit gap as a SIDBI-specific shortcoming. However, as the principal financial institution for MSME development, SIDBI is well placed to coordinate solutions, test new lending models and encourage the wider financial system to serve enterprises that remain underserved. This is where its developmental role can become even more influential. Greater Direct Lending Can Complement the Multiplier Model SIDBI’s direct portfolio recorded strong growth during FY2024-25. This indicates that the institution is already expanding its engagement with enterprises through branches, digital channels and partner-led arrangements. The next step could be a calibrated expansion of direct lending in areas where conventional financial institutions remain cautious. These may include: new-to-credit micro enterprises; businesses without substantial physical collateral; enterprises investing in modern machinery; MSMEs entering export markets; units adopting clean-energy or resource-efficient technologies; businesses supplying government departments or large corporations; women-led and first-generation enterprises; and viable businesses operating in underserved districts and industrial clusters. Such an expansion need not turn SIDBI into a conventional retail bank. Its direct products can remain demonstrative, specialised and capable of being replicated by banks and other lenders. This would be consistent with SIDBI’s stated approach of using direct lending to address credit gaps through innovative products that can subsequently be scaled by the wider financial ecosystem. Measuring the Benefit Received by the Final Borrower One of the most constructive reforms would be greater visibility into the outcomes of institutional finance. SIDBI could consider publishing aggregated information on: the categories of enterprises financed through partner institutions; the proportion of new-to-credit borrowers; the geographical distribution of lending; average sanction and disbursement timelines; the proportion of women-owned enterprises financed; the extent of collateral-free lending; and the effective financial benefit received by final borrowers. This would not require the disclosure of commercially sensitive information relating to individual borrowers or lenders. A carefully designed public-impact framework could demonstrate how institutional finance translates into enterprise growth, formalisation, employment, investment and regional development. It would also help SIDBI communicate its contribution more effectively. Making Cash-Flow-Based Lending More Widely Available Many small businesses possess viable operations but have limited physical collateral. Their financial strength may be visible through invoices, GST filings, banking transactions, digital payments, purchase orders or regular supplies to established buyers. SIDBI can play a leading role in advancing cash-flow-based credit assessment. The objective should be to enable lenders to evaluate the economic activity of an enterprise rather than relying excessively on property or other conventional security. SIDBI’s digital initiatives and knowledge products show that the institution is already investing in technology, data-led decision-making and digital interventions for the MSME sector. The opportunity is to bring these capabilities together into a more widely accessible lending architecture that responsibly uses consent-based commercial data. Such a system should maintain appropriate safeguards for data privacy, underwriting quality and borrower protection. Delayed Payments Need Coordinated Financial Solutions Delayed receivables continue to create working-capital stress for many MSMEs. SIDBI alone cannot resolve the delayed-payment problem. The issue involves buyers, government departments, public-sector enterprises, contractual arrangements, invoice acceptance, dispute-resolution mechanisms and enforcement of payment obligations. Nevertheless, SIDBI can provide important financial and institutional support. It can work with banks, TReDS platforms, large buyers, government procurement systems and industry associations to make more MSME invoices digitally visible and financeable. It could also explore carefully structured bridge-finance mechanisms for verified and accepted invoices, subject to appropriate risk controls. The objective should not be to transfer the payment obligation from buyers to a public institution. It should be to prevent otherwise viable MSMEs from experiencing avoidable liquidity stress while awaiting legitimate payments. Credit Must Be Accompanied by Capability Building The needs of an MSME rarely end with the sanctioning of a loan. Enterprises may require assistance with technology selection, quality certification, financial management, export documentation, digital adoption, productivity improvement, energy efficiency and workforce training. SIDBI’s statutory role includes promotion and development in addition to financing. It also describes credit-plus initiatives and entrepreneurial handholding as important elements of its mandate. This provides a strong foundation for a more integrated approach. A manufacturing enterprise borrowing for machinery, for example, could be connected with recognised institutions that provide: technical evaluation; workforce training; quality and sustainability certification; digital-production support; export readiness; and market-access guidance. This would improve the enterprise’s chances of success while also strengthening the quality of the lender’s portfolio. Converting Data into District-Level Action SIDBI has developed several valuable research and data initiatives, including MSME Pulse and its MSME Outlook Survey. Its research covers credit behaviour, business conditions, sustainability and the operating challenges faced by enterprises. The next opportunity is to convert national-level intelligence into more granular action. District-level and cluster-level MSME scorecards could examine: formal credit penetration; new-to-credit enterprises; average ticket sizes; collateral-free lending; women-owned business financing; technology-upgradation funding; export-credit availability; and persistent working-capital constraints. These scorecards could help identify regions where interventions are producing results and locations where additional attention is required. They could also support state governments, district administrations, industry associations and financial institutions in designing more targeted programmes. A Constructive Agenda for the Next Phase SIDBI can strengthen its developmental impact through seven complementary measures. 1. Calibrated expansion of direct lending SIDBI could gradually expand specialised direct-credit programmes for underserved enterprises, without weakening its institutional-finance model. 2. Outcome-based institutional finance Refinance and institutional lending could be accompanied by aggregated reporting on borrower categories, regional distribution and measurable benefits delivered to MSMEs. 3. Cash-flow-based assessment SIDBI can lead the responsible integration of consent-based financial and commercial information for viable enterprises that lack conventional collateral. 4. Cluster-focused intervention Branches and programmes could be evaluated through development indicators such as new enterprises financed, technology upgrades supported and employment enabled. 5. Dedicated transition finance Specialised windows could support automation, artificial intelligence, energy efficiency, clean technology, quality certification and export-market diversification. 6. Credit-plus assistance Enterprises receiving finance could be connected with approved technical, managerial, skilling and market-access institutions. 7. Periodic developmental-impact reporting A dedicated impact report could explain how SIDBI’s interventions have supported formalisation, additional credit access, employment, productivity and regional inclusion. SIDBI’s Next Opportunity SIDBI has already created a substantial financial and institutional foundation for MSME development. Its large institutional-finance portfolio, expanding direct lending, digital initiatives, knowledge products and development programmes demonstrate the breadth of its contribution. The case for a larger last-mile role should therefore not be read as criticism of SIDBI’s past work. It is an argument for building on that work. India’s next phase of growth will require micro enterprises to become stronger small businesses, small businesses to become competitive medium enterprises and medium enterprises to enter global value chains. SIDBI has the mandate and institutional position to accelerate that transition. Its greatest future contribution may come from combining the scale of institutional finance with the visibility, innovation and enterprise-level understanding associated with direct developmental engagement. The discussion should not be about choosing between indirect and direct lending. It should be about finding the right combination of scale, affordability, innovation, transparency and measurable last-mile impact. For India’s MSMEs, that combination could become a powerful catalyst for sustainable and inclusive economic growth. Editorial note: This article is an independent policy analysis based on publicly available information and official institutional reports. It acknowledges SIDBI’s contribution to MSME financing and development while presenting suggestions for strengthening its future impact. The views expressed are those of the author and are intended to encourage constructive discussion.
